Amazing game!  At first I thought it was quite linear, but the story widens as the game progresses.  Excellent twists, and a deep reflection on surveillance that takes a whole new meanings when you get your hands dirty…

Orwell is more "interesting" than it is "fun" or "good"

You play as an Investigator snooping around people's profiles and conversations in order to find a suspect and get them arrested. Some info will unlock more info as the system recognizes to snoop through that detail as well (ex: you find someone's email address, you can now check their inbox)

This gets really really clunky as it goes on. It's obviously not very clear what's gonna unearth more documents to go through, and some of the stuff you do *need* to upload isn't obvious either, so it's very easy to fall into a "throw everything blue into the machine". Only the yellow data chunks are easily marked as a choice, and there it feels like there's a 'correct' and a 'wrong' choice a lot of the times, instead of just positioning from the system.

The ending (admittedly I'm certain I got the worst ending) feels hollow because suddenly two characters just blab and give you a single choice to go through. The part where you're limited to 20 data chunks before the day goes through should've been incorporated way back in the story - as it forces you to think a lot more on what you're uploading. I understand it could've locked people away from progress, however.

Character writing is either okay or awful in this. Some of the characters are terrible and feel unbelievable as people, others feel true to life.

Anyway, the game is worth your time if you're interested in this debate and you're getting it for real cheap. The idea has been explored in several other works in a better way I feel, but the mechanics in here are very interesting.

This game comes from the same niche genre as Papers, Please, in which you operate as a government official tasked with keeping your country "safe" in a dystopian, high-surveillance world. It's a breath of fresh air in what I hope to be a more well-explored type of gameplay and setup. Instead of being the person to dismantle The System with guns a-blazing, you are a body warming your seat at a desk and following through with what your superiors ask of you--namely, monitoring and surveillance of certain individuals suspected of being involved in recent terrorist attacks in your country's capital. While many might find this to be a boring game, for us info-hunters and online archive fiends, this is exactly up our alley (and regardless, many people found themselves plenty surprised with how engaging Papers, Please was despite it being literal desk duty). The process of determining the relevant information from the chaff is an exercise in your detective work; conflicting bits of information challenges your ability to intuit context and intent, the results of your choices ultimately influencing the file you are compiling for your superiors, who can only draw conclusions based on it. Since they are depending on you to be diligent and honest, you are responsible for their ultimate decision on how to proceed at the end of the day. The interface is smooth, streamlined, and well-organized; your overseer Symes and his commentary on your findings is a tiny light in what would otherwise be a soul-sucking experience (at the end of the day, you are cutting your Persons of Interest into tiny bits of info); the music is an understated, mechanical heartbeat similar to Massive Attack's "Teardrop on Fire", famously used as the theme for the show House, M.D.. And at the end of the day, your choices matter. Only complaint is that sometimes your brain is thinking farther ahead than the game. There are several times when I thought "Wait, I remember who this is. I might as well jump on it upload a profile pic and the info from that file I found on them" but discovered I had to wait until the game found them relevant enough to devote any attention to them. I love this game and what it has to offer, and if anything I've said has piqued your interest, I pretty much guarantee you won't be disappointed.

Absolutely amazing if you're interested in the ethics of surveillance and social media. It mostly plays as an interactive novel which might be a turn off for some but otherwise I absolutely recommend this.

Orwell does one thing very well: it accurately simulates the tedium inherent in most government jobs. If you ever wanted to know what it's like to work at the DMV or IRS, Orwell is your game. The simplistic click-and-drag gameplay might have been mitigated by an interesting story or characters, but Orwell's plot is boilerplate paranoia fiction delivered in screen after screen of dull exposition. The puzzle design vacillates between the extremes of baffingly obtuse and blaringly obvious. At several points, I found myself simply clicking through every single screen and selecting every random bit of data I could simply to progress the story.

On the plus side, the ambient soundtrack is pleasant and includes the occasional dramatic sting to highlight twists in the storyline. The Orwell UI is clean and easy to navigate. I also think that the developers had the best of intentions to create a game that grapples with the rise of the surveillance state in modern societies.

Unfortunately, good intentions don't trump bad game design. Stay away from Borewell.

I got this game for free through humble bundle during the giveaway period so I thought "Ehh, why not?".

I was genuinely surprised. This game is SO DAMN GOOD.
I'm still at chapter 3 of the game but I'll update this once I finish it.
So, here's a detailed rundown so far:

Story:
The game starts out with a cinematic that introduces the world and how it advanced it is in terms of technology. You will play as a rookie investigator of sorts who will undergo a basic test of performance. Here, it lays out your role and responsibilities clearly without being overly confusing. After all the introductions, the actual story starts. The story is INTENSE. It tries to confuse you but you want more of it. And the urge just doesn't stop until you get clearance. Especially where your choices matter.

Characters:
The characters feel alive. You can tell that a lot of work has been put into these characters as you get to know their backgrounds, way of thinking, motives, goals, etc. Heck, I even relate and sympathize with some of these characters.

Sound:
Sometimes so relaxing like you had a good day at work. Sometimes so intense that you want to scream "Damn this scroll bar!!!!11" as you race against time scrolling down frantically looking the datachunk (piece of information) in hopes that it may change the potential outcome. Sometimes grim when you find out secrets that the characters themselves never mentions.

UI:
I love the simplistic yet futuristic UI design and world setting. It helps keep you immersed in the game which revolves around you, the player, acting as an investigator from when you start the game and through your whole playthrough.

Overall:
Still on the edge of my seat while writing this review. This game is very well-made. The world is solidly built, the characters feel alive, the soundtrack enhances the gameplay, and the UI fits into the setting extremely well. If you have played hacknet, emily is away, or similar games, then this game shares a resemblance to those. It's a very personal experience and a very pleasant one at that.


Is the game worth it? If you like immersing yourself in stories, absolutely.
